summary:
The machines we left behind can still teach us how to explore. We built Silent Explorers, an interactive learning website where kids ages 8–14 can spin 3D globes of the Moon and Mars and tap nine sites to discover the equipment still there.

At each stop, the machine tells its own story. NASA mission records and images show what really happened, while games, animations, and a comic give kids more ways to explore. The site is available in English and Ukrainian.

By telling the stories of equipment left behind, Silent Explorers helps kids see how science works through real missions. They learn what questions scientists asked, how spacecraft gathered evidence, and what that evidence helped us discover.
details:
Silent Explorers is an interactive learning website for kids ages 8–14. Visitors choose the Moon or Mars, spin a 3D globe, and tap a marker to discover one of nine sites where mission equipment remains. Each marker opens a card with a story told from the machine’s point of view, a mission log, and an explanation of what scientists learned. Some cards also include a mini-game, animation, comic, or interactive panorama. Kids can track their discoveries and earn an Explorer badge by visiting all nine sites.

We wanted kids to see how discoveries happen. In the Pathfinder mini-game, they try an airbag landing to see how the mission reached the surface of Mars. In the Spirit panorama explorer, they look around real rover images and tap landmarks to find out what scientists noticed there. Teachers can use individual mission cards as short classroom activities, and kids can explore at their own pace in English or Ukrainian.

We built the site with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Three.js for the globes and HTML Canvas for the games. We used FFmpeg to prepare videos and GitHub Pages to host the site. A list of missions gives visitors another way to open the cards, including on devices where the 3D view is unavailable.

We considered how to make mission science easy to follow while keeping the details accurate. For example, the Opportunity card explains what a sol is before comparing the rover’s planned and actual mission lengths. We checked mission details against NASA sources and labeled artistic reconstructions so visitors can tell them apart from archival images.
